subject: 4FAFE46E3FC7417BAC3D18A3C7D260C2
introduction: These readings tell, largely in the words of those who lived it, how Bahá’u’lláh and his companions were banished in 1868 to the prison city of ‘Akká: the voyage and the jeering arrival, sickness in the barracks, years in small houses under guard, the first pilgrims finding a way in, the garden and the mansion outside the walls where the confinement at last gave way, and the later conviction that the exile had served the cause it was meant to end. A hundred of the guide's hundred and seven quotations are read here beside a hundred from elsewhere. Nearly all stand alongside, since prison and exile have a long literature: Joseph and Jeremiah, the Psalms of captivity, Paul's letters from his chains and the friends who sought him out, John on Patmos, Dante on the bread of exile, Lovelace, Cowper and Keats on the country after the town, the prophets on the desert made a garden. Nine push back or add a side: a psalm from the pit that never reaches praise, John the Baptist doubting in prison, Wilde's bricks of shame, Byron's prisoner sighing at his release, God's pity for Nineveh beside the phrase 'the most wicked of all people', and Jesus on the tower in Siloam beside the reading that connects cholera with a holy presence.
questions: Which details of the arrival and the barracks stay with you, and why were they recorded?
Bahá’u’lláh named the place the Most Great Prison and later called it a paradise. Compare Paul's 'prisoner of the Lord' and Lovelace's stone walls. What makes such renaming honest?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the days in prison were pleasant. Wilde wrote that prisons are built with bricks of shame. What does each know that the other might not?
The people of ‘Akká are called the most wicked of all people, and the city is later said to be transformed. How does the question put to Jonah about Nineveh bear on this?
One reading links the absence of cholera to Bahá’u’lláh's presence. How does Jesus on the tower in Siloam caution a reader?
'If He had not been banished, the Tablets to the kings would not have been revealed.' When is it right to read a wrong as having served a purpose?

outside.why: The Qur'an recalls a like hour for Muhammad: they plot to kill thee or to drive thee forth; they plot, but God also plots.
Dante was told what exile would mean: to abandon everything most beloved, and to learn how salt is the bread of others.
A psalm speaks of the pestilence that walks in darkness, and of a thousand falling at one's side.
Jeremiah was let down by cords into a dungeon with no water, only mire, and sank in it.
Acts tells of the day a great persecution fell on the church at Jerusalem, and all were scattered abroad.
The second psalm sees rulers take counsel together against the Lord and his anointed.
A psalm asks the question the exiles' journey answers: who will bring me into the strong city, who will lead me?
Hosea promised that a valley whose name means trouble, Achor, would be given for a door of hope.
Joseph was put into the prison where the king's prisoners were bound, and the Lord was with him there.
A psalm says that they that go down to the sea in ships see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep.
Paul lists his journeys: thrice shipwrecked, in perils of waters, of robbers, of his own countrymen.
Hebrews remembers those who had trial of mockings, bonds and imprisonment, and wandered destitute.
Peter was kept in prison, while prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him.
A psalmist says: all they that see me laugh me to scorn; they shoot out the lip, they shake the head.
Isaiah's servant is despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows from whom faces are hidden.
The exiles in Babylon sat down by the rivers and wept when they remembered Zion.
Lamentations gives the prisoner's sentence: he hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out.
Wilde wrote of a prisoner's wistful eye turned on that little tent of blue which prisoners call the sky.
A psalm prays: let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; preserve those that are appointed to die.
A voice in Lamentations calls on the name of the Lord out of the low dungeon, and is heard.
Elijah in hiding lived on the bread the ravens brought him, and drank of the brook.
Israel in the wilderness came to Marah and could not drink the bitter waters until they were made sweet.
Jesus said that foxes have holes and birds have nests, but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
Acts ends with Paul dwelling two whole years in his own hired house, receiving all who came to him.
Hebrews asks its readers to remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them.
A psalm that never turns to praise says: thou hast laid me in the lowest pit; I am shut up, and I cannot come forth. What does such a voice add to accounts of patience in prison?
An earlier royal decree against a scattered people began with the charge that their laws were different from all others.
Paul writes that he suffers as an evildoer, even unto bonds, but the word of God is not bound.
Joseph in the Qur'an says: O my Lord, prison is more dear to me than that to which they urge me.
John the Baptist, in prison, sent to ask Jesus: art thou he that should come, or do we look for another? What does long confinement do to certainty?
Jesus counts it as done to himself: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.
The Qur'an praises those who feed the needy, the orphan and the prisoner for the love of God, wanting no thanks.
Paul blesses Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of his chain but sought him out very diligently in Rome, and found him.
Paul thanks God at every remembrance of his friends at Philippi, and prays for them with joy.
A pilgrim psalm says: my soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the Lord.
Paul, beaten and jailed without trial, would not be released quietly: let the magistrates come themselves and fetch us out.
Jesus told the disciple who drew a sword to put it up, for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
When disciples wished fire on a hostile village, Jesus rebuked them: ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
Isaiah says that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come, and no man lays it to heart.
Paul says that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
A psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Cowper said the same in a line: God made the country, and man made the town.
Keats wrote that to one long in city pent it is very sweet to look into the fair and open face of heaven.
The Song of Songs greets the green again: the winter is past, the flowers appear on the earth.
Isaiah promises that the Lord will make the wilderness of Zion like Eden, her desert like a garden.
Bacon opens his essay on gardens: God Almighty first planted a garden, and it is the purest of human pleasures.
Byron's prisoner of Chillon grew friends with his chains, and regained his freedom with a sigh. Why might a prisoner be slow to leave?
Wordsworth says that the prison to which we doom ourselves is no prison.
Lovelace held that stone walls do not a prison make for one whose soul is free.
In Acts the iron gate that leads into the city opens to Peter of its own accord.
Isaiah hears the word given to prisoners: go forth; and to them that are in darkness: shew yourselves.
A psalm prays: bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name.
A psalm of release says: then was our mouth filled with laughter; the Lord hath done great things for us.
Hebrews remembers Abraham sojourning in a strange country, dwelling in tents, looking for a city with foundations.
Joseph told the brothers who sold him: ye thought evil against me, but God meant it unto good.
Gamaliel warned the council to take heed what they did to these men.
Paul asks Timothy to bring with him the cloak he left at Troas, and the books and parchments.
The Song of Songs has the beloved say: I am come into my garden.
Isaiah pictures the hills breaking into singing and all the trees of the field clapping their hands.
A psalm has the field be joyful, and all the trees of the wood rejoice before the Lord.
The rose of this coast is in the Song of Songs: I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys.
Isaiah names the country round about: the excellency of Carmel and Sharon shall see the glory of the Lord.
Ecclesiastes counts it the gift of God that a man should eat and drink and enjoy the good of all his labour.
Nehemiah kept a holy day the same way: eat the fat, drink the sweet, and send portions to those with nothing.
Wilde wrote that every prison men build is built with bricks of shame. Can a prison be remembered as pleasant without forgetting what prisons do?
A psalmist remembers God upon his bed and meditates on him in the night watches.
The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name.
Lamentations, of all books, says that the Lord's compassions are new every morning.
Paul's rule was to rejoice evermore, pray without ceasing, and in every thing give thanks.
Paul turned his chains into a title, writing as 'the prisoner of the Lord'.
John names his place of banishment at the head of his book: I was in the isle that is called Patmos.
Paul signs a letter with his own hand and three words: remember my bonds.
Isaiah's servant is oppressed and afflicted, brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and opens not his mouth.

When Jonah wished Nineveh destroyed, God asked: should not I spare that great city, with its sixscore thousand who cannot tell right hand from left? How should the people of a 'wicked' city be regarded?
Nathanael asked whether any good thing can come out of Nazareth, and was told: come and see. What do a town's reputation and its future have to do with each other?
Micah addresses a town little among the thousands of Judah, out of which a ruler shall come.
Isaiah says that the wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad, and the desert shall blossom as the rose.
A psalmist says to God: thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing, and girded me with gladness.
Milton has a speaker claim that the mind is its own place, and can make a heaven of hell.
Isaiah says of this same coast that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
The phrase is the Qur'an's: Our word unto a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say unto it: Be! and it is.
Elisha cast salt into a town's bad spring and said: thus saith the Lord, I have healed these waters.
Ezekiel foresees passers-by saying: this land that was desolate is become like the garden of Eden.
Jesus said that God sends rain on the just and on the unjust. How far can a town's health be read as a sign of who lives in it?
Jesus denied that the eighteen killed by the tower in Siloam were sinners above others. What care is needed in reading an epidemic as a judgment or a sign?
Isaiah says of the servant that he shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street.
Hebrews says of the patriarchs that they confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
The Qur'an says: fain would they put out the light of God with their mouths, but God will perfect his light.
Tertullian told the persecutors of his day that the oftener Christians are mown down, the more they grow.
Thoreau wrote that under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. What does a penal colony say about those sent there, and about those who send them?
Jesus lamented over Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to her.
John's Gospel says that the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not.
A psalm says that the stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.
The Qur'an keeps the words spoken on that departure: grieve not; lo, God is with us.
Jesus told his disciples that they would weep while the world rejoiced, but their sorrow would be turned into joy.
Paul wrote from prison that the things which happened to him had fallen out rather to the furtherance of the gospel.
The Qur'an tells of a queen who received a noble letter from Solomon, calling her not to exalt herself but to come.
Tradition preserves Muhammad's letter to Heraclius, the ruler of Byzantium, inviting him to the right path.
Jesus told his disciples they would be brought before governors and kings, for a testimony.
Paul calls himself an ambassador in bonds, and asks prayer that he may speak boldly as he ought.

timothy-not-ashamed-of-my-chain.text: The Lord give mercy unto the house of Onesiphorus; for he oft refreshed me, and was not ashamed of my chain: But, when he was in Rome, he sought me out very diligently, and found me

acts-let-them-come-themselves.text: But Paul said unto them, They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans, and have cast us into prison; and now do they thrust us out privily? nay verily; but let them come themselves and fetch us out

acts-his-own-hired-house.text: And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him, Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching those things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, no man forbidding him

psalm-strong-city.text: Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom

psalm-laugh-me-to-scorn.text: All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, He trusted on the Lord that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him

song-rose-of-sharon.text: I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys. As the lily among thorns, so is my love among the daughters

revelation-isle-called-patmos.text: I John, who also am your brother, and companion in tribulation, and in the kingdom and patience of Jesus Christ, was in the isle that is called Patmos, for the word of God, and for the testimony of Jesus Christ

ephesians-ambassador-in-bonds.text: And for me, that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, For which I am an ambassador in bonds: that therein I may speak boldly, as I ought to speak

isaiah-taken-away-from-the-evil-to-come.text: The righteous perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart: and merciful men are taken away, none considering that the righteous is taken away from the evil to come

psalm-go-down-to-the-sea.text: They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; These see the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep

isaiah-prisoners-go-forth.text: That thou mayest say to the prisoners, Go forth; to them that are in darkness, Shew yourselves. They shall feed in the ways, and their pastures shall be in all high places

acts-iron-gate.text: When they were past the first and the second ward, they came unto the iron gate that leadeth unto the city; which opened to them of his own accord: and they went out, and passed on through one street; and forthwith the angel departed from him

lamentations-hedged-me-about.text: He hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out: he hath made my chain heavy

psalm-lowest-pit.text: Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah. Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth

isaiah-wilderness-like-eden.text: For the Lord shall comfort Zion: he will comfort all her waste places; and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her desert like the garden of the Lord; joy and gladness shall be found therein, thanksgiving, and the voice of melody

kings-ravens-brought-him-bread.text: And the ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook

colossians-remember-my-bonds.text: The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace be with you

quran-fellow-prisoners.text: O my fellow-prisoners! Are divers lords better, or Allah the One, Almighty?

dante-bread-of-others.text: Thou shalt abandon everything beloved / Most tenderly, and this the arrow is / Which first the bow of banishment shoots forth. / Thou shalt have proof how savoureth of salt / The bread of others, and how hard a road / The going down and up another's stairs
dante-bread-of-others.author: Dante Alighieri

cowper-god-made-the-country.text: God made the country, and man made the town
cowper-god-made-the-country.author: William Cowper

keats-long-in-city-pent.text: To one who has been long in city pent, / 'T is very sweet to look into the fair / And open face of heaven,—to breathe a prayer / Full in the smile of the blue firmament
keats-long-in-city-pent.author: John Keats
keats-long-in-city-pent.work: To one who has been long in city pent
